examples.input: start watching with no directory option and no TROUPE_THEATRE variable, from /home/sam/show

results.1: the line names `/home/sam/show`, the full path of the current folder
the line names `../stage`, exactly as typed
results.2: the line names `../stage`, exactly as typed

results.1: the line names `/var/shows`, not the system's real path `/private/var/shows`
results.2: the line names `/var/shows`, not the system's real path `/private/var/shows`

context.in_practice: Routes 1 and 2 only differ when the user gives no directory. In that case route 1 shows the real full path, so a log or screenshot shows which folder was watched. Route 2 shows `.`, which only makes sense if you know where the command was run. When a directory is given, both routes print it exactly as typed, relative parts included, and neither turns it into the system's real path. Route 3 is only a placeholder: nobody considered it, so it describes no behaviour.
context.stakes: When the tool starts watching, it prints a line naming the directory it is watching. That line is how a user confirms the tool is looking at the right place, and whether it is useful depends on whether the path is unambiguous and recognisable.
context.tradeoff: Route 1 costs one extra lookup of the current folder, which buys a clear line when no directory is given. Route 2 is the simplest, but the default case only says `.`. Route 3 defines nothing.

plan_why: The routes only differ in the `watching <dir>` line printed by `troupe config watch`, which runs until SIGINT/SIGTERM. Watch is forbidden in this sandbox and would hit the 20-second limit, and no other command prints the theatre directory, so the difference between the absolute cwd (route 1) and '.' (route 2) can't be shown.
routes: --theatre or TROUPE_THEATRE as given; the absolute cwd when neither is set
